IPC CPU
Shared Storage
Shared files might be the most basic method of IPC. A producer can write to a file and consumer can read from it. The main issue is preventing race conditions as both procs could access the same data. To prevent this, we can lock the file as follows:

The producer must gain an exclusive lock to write to a file
The consumer can gain a shared lock which would allow other readers to also read but exclude the writer from writing.

Usually the locking is done using fcntl which accepts a file descriptor. Note that different programs may have different file descriptors that still point to the same physical file. Linux also provides a function flock which is a thin wrapper of fcntl. This also allows you to either lock the whole file or certain bytes of the file.

lit-notes/general/Cache-Coherence.title: Cache Coherence
lit-notes/general/Cache-Coherence.content:
cache-coherence CPU
Intro
When having a multi-core architecture you have several cores that shared a variable but still have their own cache. This synchronization between caches can be tricky because two cores may view the same variable differently due to the different caches. The difficulty is generally referred to as the cache coherence problem.
informally, a system is coherent if ant read of a data item returns the most recently written value of that item. This can be broken into two aspect:

Coherence - defines what values can be returned by a read
Consistency - determines when a written value will be returned by a read

Coherency
A memory system is coherent if
(1) A read by core P to location X that follows a write by P to X with no writes of X by other cores occurring between the write and read, always returns the value written by P to X.
(2) A read by a core to location X that follows a write by another core to X returns the written value, if the read and write are sufficiently separated in time and no other writes to X occur between the two accesses.
(3) Writes to the same location are serialised. That means, two writes to the same location by any core are seen in the same order by all cores. For example, if CPU B writes 2 to X after time step 3, cores can never read the value at X as 2 and then later read it as 1
Basic Schemes For Enforcing Coherence
The caches usually provide both migration and replication of shared data items.
Migration - A data item can be moved to a local cache and used there in a transparent manner. Migration reduces both the latency and access a shared data item that is allocated remotely and the bandwidth demand n the shared memory.
Replication - When shared data are being concurrently read, the caches make a copy of the data into the location cache. Replication reduces both the latency of access and contention of a read for a shared item
These two tools are so important that many processors implement these in hardware to maintain coherent caches. The protocols are called cache-coherent protocols. A key element to their implementation is tracking the state of any sharing of a data block.
The most popular protocol is snooping. Every cache that has a copy of the data from a block of physical memory also has a copy of the sharing status of the block, but no centralized state is kept. The caches are all accessible via some broadcast (data bus or network) and all cache controllers monitor or snoop on the medium to determine whether they have a copy of a data block that is requested on the bus/switch.
Snooping Protocols
One method to ensure coherence is to have a core have exclusive rights to a data block. This style of protocol is called a write invalidate protocol because it invalidates copies in other caches on a write.
Exclusive access ensures that no other readable/writable copies of an item exist when the write occurs. Thus, a read after this exclusive right would cause a cache miss and would have core B request a copy from Core A (assuming core A did the write and B had a local copy) which would then be sent over the data bus/network.
If two cores do try to write at the same time, because this ex is atomic, one of them will win and the other core will have to way and also obtain a new copy of the data first. Therefore this protocol also enforces write serialisation.

lit-notes/general/Coherence-Basics.title: Coherence Basics
lit-notes/general/Coherence-Basics.content:
cache-coherence CPU
primer2020_2nd_edition
Baseline System Model
We consider a system with multiple processors and a shared memory. The cores can perform loads and stores to all (physical) addresses. Each core has its own private cache and a last-level cache (LLC) which is shared by all the cores. Cache will refer to as the private cache and not the LLC unless said otherwise.
How Incoherence Could Possibly Occur
The rise of this issue comes from one fundamental problem: there exists multiple access with access to caches and memory. In modern systems, the actors are the cores, DMA engines and external devices that can read/write to caches and memory (though we primarily focus on cores).
Incoherence would occur when two or more cores have a copy of the same variable and one or more of the cores have a wrong copy of it. To solve this issue, we introduce cache coherent protocols that make the store from core A visible to core B.
The Cache Coherence Interface
Informally, the goal is for a write to be made visible to all other cores. The cores interact with the coherence protocol via a coherence interface that provides two methods:

Read-request - takes in a memory location as a param and returns a value
Write-request - accept a memory location and value and returns an Ack.

There are many different protocols in nature and we tend to put them into two categories based on the nature of their coherence interfaces - specifically based on whether there is a clean separation of coherence from the consistency model or whether they are indivisible.
Consistency-Agnostic Coherence
In the first category, a write is made visible to other cores before returning.  Because write are propagated synchronously, the interface is identical to that of an atomic memory system with no cache. Thus any system interacting with it can treat it as atomic memory with no cache present. This interface provides a nice separation of concerns. The cache coherence protocol abstracts away the caches completely and only the memory is contained within the coherence box.
Consistency-directed Coherence
This is a more recent category where write are propagated asynchronously. A write can thus return before it has been made visible to all cores, allowing for stale values to be observed. However, in order to correctly enforce consistency, the coherence protocols in this class must ensure that the order in which writes are eventually made visible adheres to the ordering rules of the consistency model.
This category emerged to support throughput-based GPGPU.
Consistency-Agnostic Coherence Invariants
What invariant must coherence protocols satisfy to make the caches invisible and present abstraction of an atomic system.
A coherence through the single-write-multiple-reader invariant is that for any given memory location at any given moment, there is either a single core that may write to it or some number of cores that may read it. Thus, there is never a time when a given memory location may be written by one core and simultaneously read or written to by any other cores.
In addition to SWMR, the data must be propagated correctly. This is important because if a write happens, all the other cores that have a, now stale, copy in their own cache, must be notified and invalidate and fetch the fresh copy of the new value.

lit-notes/memory/CUDA-Runtime.title: CUDA Runtime
lit-notes/memory/CUDA-Runtime.content:
cuda Memory-Model
CUDA_C_Programming_Guide
Device Memory
The cuda runtime assumes a heterogeneous system with a host (CPU) and a device (GPU). Kernels work with device memory which is separate from host memory, which means that you must do own mallocs and transfers from host to device and back. Device memory can be either

Linear memory
CUDA arrays

cuda arrays are opaque memory layouts optimized for texture fetching. Linear memory is allocated in a single unified address space which means that different entities can reference one another via pointers. The size of the address space depends on the host and compute capability of the GPU.
For N-dimensional arrays it is recommended to use cudaMallocPitch() and cudaMalloc3D() instead of cudaMalloc() as the former add appropriate padding for alignment
Device Memory L2 Access Management
When a cuda kernel calls global data repeatedly, such accesses can be considered to be persiting. One the other hand, if is accesses once, it is considered to be streaming
L2 Cache Set-Aside for Persisting Accesses
A portion of the L2 cache can be set aside for persisting data accesses. The persisting data has priority in the L2 cache and for example, the streaming data can only enter if the L2 cache is not full of persisting data.
When the GPU is configured in Multi-instance GPU (MIG) mode, this feature is turned off.
L2 Policy for Persisting Accesses
An accesses policy window specifies a contiguous region of global memory and persistence property in the L2 cache for accesses within that region.
L2 Access Properties
There are three types of different global memory data access:

cudaAccessPropertyStreaming - mem accesses that occur with the streaming property are less likely to be L2 cached because they are often evicted.
cudaAccessPropertyPersisting - mem access that occur with the persisting property are more likely to persist in the L2 because of the set-aside portion of the L2
cudaAccessPropertyNormal - This access property resets the previously applied property. Mem accesses with persisting property from the previous cuda kernels may be retained in the L2 long after intended use. This works as a pallet cleanser.

Reset L2 Access to Normal
A persisting L2 cache from a previous kernel may persist in the L2. Hence a reset to normal is important for streaming or normal mem accesses to utilize the cache with normal priority. Two ways this can be done:

Reset previous mem region with the access property cudaAccessPropertyNormal
Reset all persisting L2 cache lines to normal using cudaCtxResetPersistingL2Cache()
Eventually untouched lines reset to normal. This is strongly discouraged

Manage Utilization of L2 Set-Aside Cache
Multiple kernels executing concurrently in different cuda streams may have different access policies. However, the L2 set-aside portion is shared among all the kernels. A result is the sum of all concurrent individual use. The benefit is that persisting diminish as the volume of persisting accesses exceeds the L2 cache capacity.
To manage the utilization of the L2 set-aside, one must consider the following:

size of the L2 set-aside cache
kernels that are concurrently executing
Access policy of the other kernels
When and how the L2 reset is required to allow normal streaming access.

Shared Memory
shared mem is allocated using the __shared__ attribute. This mem is much fast than global memory as mentioned in CUDA Programming Model. It can be used as scratchpad memory (software managed cache) to minimize global mem access.
The following code is an example
__global__
void reduce_naive(const int *d_in, int *d_out, int n) {
 
	size_t index = (blockDim.x * blockIdx.x + threadIdx.x);
		if (index < n) {
		__shared__ int buffer[1024];
		buffer[index] = d_in[index];
		__syncthreads();
		
		for (int stride = 1; stride < blockDim.x; stride*=2) {
			if (index % (2*stride) == 0) {
				buffer[index] = buffer[index] + buffer[index+stride];
			
			__syncthreads();
			d_out[index] = buffer[index];
	    }
	}
 
}
Distributed Shared Memory
Thread block clusters allow threads in a block cluster to access shared mem of all participating threads. This partition is called dsitributed memory access and the corresponding address space is called distributed shared memoery address space.  Threads that belong to block cluster can read/write or perform atomics regardless whether the data belongs to the local thread block. Whether the kernel uses static or dynamic me is up to the thread block. The size of the distributed mem is
\text{thread blocks} \times \text{size of shared mem per block}. Accessing this data requires all thread blocks to exist. A use can guarantee that by using cluster.sync(). The user also needs to ensure that the mem operations happen before the exit of  block.
Memory Sync Domains
Some cuda kernels me see degraded performance due to fence/flush operations which are needed to enforce the memory model.
Isolating Traffic with Domains
Beginning with the Hopper architecture, we have ways to alleviate such inter fences. In exchange for explicit assitance from code, the GPU can reduce the net case by a fence operations. Eacg kernel launch has a domain ID. Writes and fences are tagged with the ID and a fence will only order writes matching the fence’s domain.
When using domains, code must abide by the rule that ordering or sync between distinct domains on the same GPU requires system-scope fencing. Within a domain, device-scope fencing remains sufficient. This is necessary for cumulative as one kernel’s writes will not be encompassed by a fence in a diff domain.
Using Domains in Cuda
Domains are accessible via the launch attribute cudaLaunchAttributeMemSyncDomain and cudaLaunchAttributeMemSynchDomainMap. The latter provides a mapping from logical to physical domains.
The remote domain is intended for kernels performing remote memory access.
Async Concurrent Execution
Cuda exposes the following operations that can work concurrently with one another:

Computation on the host
Computation on the device
Memory transfers from host to device and vise versa
Memory transfers within the memory of a given device and among devices

Concurrent Operations Between Host & Device
Concurrent host execution are done through an sync lib that returns control to the host thread before the device completes the task. Using async calls, many device operations can be queued together to be executed by the cuda driver. This relieves the host thread of managing the device. The following are async with w.r.t host:

Kernel launches
Mem copies withing the device
Mem copies from host to device of block less than 64KB
Mem copies by functions with the Async prefix
Mem set function calls.

Concurrent Kernel Launches
Some devices can execute multiple concurrent kernels. The max number of kernel launches depends on the compute capability of the device. A kernel from one cuda context cannot execute concurrently with a kernel from a diff context. If the user wants to run multiple kernels from multiple procs. simultaneously on one SM, one must enable MPS.
Explicit Sync
One way is to use cudaDeviceSynchronize() which waits until the preceding commands in all streams of all host threads have completed.
cudaStreamSynchronize() takes stream as an input and waits until that stream has synchronized.
cudaStreamWaitEvent() takes and Cuda Event as an input and waits fir the event to be done.
Unified Virtual Address Space
When the application runs as a 64-but proc. a single address soace is used for the host and devices. All host mem allocations made via the cuda API and all device mem allocations are within the virtual space. As a result:

The location of any me  on the host allocated through cuda or on the device use the unified address space, can be determined by the value of the pointer using cudaPointerGetAttributes()
When copying to/from mem of a any device using this address space, the cudaMemcpyKind param of cudaMemcpy*() is set to default to determine locations from the pointers. This also works for host pointers not allocated using cuda as long as the current device uses the unified mem.
Allocations via cudaHostAlloc() are automatically portable to all devices and pointers returned by this func can be directly used with the kernel running on these devices.

Inter-process Communication
Any device pointer or event handle created by a host thread can directly be referenced by other threads within the same proc. It is not valid outside of the proc. and cannot be directly referenced by threads of other procs.
To combat this and shared pointers and event across procs one must use the IPC API. The IPC API is only supported for 64-bit systems on Linux. Note: the IPC API is not supported for the cudaMallocManaged allocations.
Using this API, a kernel can get the IPC handle for a given device pointer using cudaIpcGetMemHandle(), pass it to another proc. using standard IPC mechanism (e.g. teleprocess shared memory or files) and use CudaIpcOpenMemHandle() to retrieve a device point from the IPC handle.
Noe that cudaMalloc() may return a pointer of a block while the IPC handle will return the entire block and lead to information disclosure between procs. To prevent this, it is important to share allocations with a 2MB alligned size.

lit-notes/memory/GPU-Memory-Consistency.title: GPU Memory Consistency
lit-notes/memory/GPU-Memory-Consistency.content:
Memory-Model cache-coherence GPU
primer2020_2nd_edition

Consistency and Coherence for Heterogeneous Systems
Most systems today are not only CPUs, they also have accelerators, the most common one being the GPU (recently however, TPU and other neural accelerators or FPGAs have become more common). These systems are referred to as heterogenous systems. The challenge becomes how can we synchronize and communicate within and across the accelerators. One trend is to expose a global shared memory interface across the CPU and the accelerator.
We assume that CPUs and GPUs have their own private physical shared memory that can be accessed via an API. Usually, each core has it owns private L1 cache and a shared L2 cache.  They (CPU, & GPU) may also have a memory-side last-level-cache, that is usually non-inclusive.
The shared memory poses an important question: how does the L1 and L2 cache across the host and device synchronize and how are their caches coherent.
GPU Consistency And Coherence
We first start by understanding briefly the GPU architecture.

Early days
GPUs, originally, we made for parallel graphics workloads. This mend that a workload involve computing independently each of the pixels that constitute the display. Thus, the workloads are characterized by a very high degree of data-parallel and low degree of data shared, synchronization and communication.
GPU Architecture
GPUs, have tens of cores called Streaming multiprocessors (SM). Each SM has many many warps with each warp consisting of 32 threads (all threads in a warp share the same program counter, and stack). The threads mapped to an SM all share the same L1 cache and a local scratchpad memory. All of the SMs share an L2 cache.  Even though threads in a warp share the same PC, they can still execute independent thread-specific paths using mask bits which specify which threads are active and which ones should not execute, know as Single Instruction Multiple Threads (SIMT).
GPU Programming Model
Analogous to the CPU Instruction Set Architecture, the GPU also has a virtual ISA. NVIDIA’s virtual ISA, for example is known as Parallel Thread Execution (PTX). CUDA, for example, is the high level abstraction that then gets compiled to the NVIDIA ISA.
CUDA, chooses to expose its hierarchical nature to the programmer via a thread hierarchy know as scopes.  Unlike CPU threads that are unique treated as “equal”, GPU threads are clustered together into Cooperative Thread Arrays (CTA). A CTA scope refers to the set of threads from the same CTA. These threads are guaranteed to be mapped to the same SM and hence share the same L1 Cache. Thus, CTAs are mapped to the same memory hierarchy level implicitly (the L1) cache. A GPU score refers to the set of threads on the same GPU. They could be from different CTAs and share the L2 cache. Thus the GPU scope is implicitly the L2 cache scope. A system scope refers to all the threads across the host and device. Thus the system scope is implicitly mapped to the LLC or unified shared memory if there is no shared LLC.
How can two threads belonging to different CTAs sync? This is what GPU consistency is all about.
GPU Consistency
GPUs support relaxed memory consistency model which (similarly to CPUs) allow for store and load operations to be reordered and tend to be organised using FENCE instructions. However, because of the lack of a Cache Coherence in a GPU, the FENCE semantics are different. Remember that the FENCE instruction in a CPU insures that a load and store must happen before the fence
// assuming x = 7
y = load(x)
y+=1
store(x, y)
load(x)
print(x) // could be 7 or 8

y = load(x)
y+=1
store(x, y)
FENCE
load(x)
print(x) // must be 8

A GPU FENCE provides similar semantics but only with respect to other threads belonging to the same CTA. A corollary of this is that the GPU store is not atomic. This means that in a GPU a store may become visible to a thread belonging to the same CTA before other threads.
GPGPU Consistency & Coherence
We have defined what consistency and coherence is for GPUs, now we need to implement it. One way would be to use a multicore CPU-like approach (using spoofing and MESI for example). However they are ill-suited for GPUs for two main reasons:

The CPU-like cache invalidation would amount to a crazy amount of traffic overhead on the GPU. That is because the aggregate of all the L1 caches tend to be greater than the size of the L2 cache. A standalone inclusive directory would not only incur a large are overhead due to duplicate tags, it would also have a high complexity. On the other hand, the embedded inclusive directory would result in significant of recall traffic upon eviction.
Because GPUs have thousands of active threads, there is a need to track a correspondingly high number of coherence transactions, which would cost significant overhead.

Without writer-initiated invalidation, how can a store propagate to other non-local L1 caches. It will be mentioned later the proposal of a self-invalidation where a process invalidates a line in its local cache to ensure that the stores from other threads become visible. The book argues that such a protocol efficiently enforces a relaxed consistency model directly rather than enforcing a consistency-agnostic invariant such as the SWMR invariant.
Temporal Coherence
The key idea is that each reader brings a cache block for a finite period of time called the lease, at the end of which, the block is self-invalidated. There are two variants: (1) a consistency-agnostic variant that enforces SWMR, in which a writer stalls until the lease of the block expires; and (2) a more efficient consistency-directed variant that enforces a relaxed memory model, where FENCE stalls. We assume that the L2 cache is inclusive: a block not represented by the L2 implies it is not in any local L1. We also assume that L1 uses a write-through/no write-allocate policy (writers must write directly to the L2 (write-through) and a write to a block that is not present in the L1 does not allocate a block in the L1)
Consistency-Agnostic Temporal Coherence
Instead of invalidating on a write, protocol has a writer wait until all of the shares have evicted the block before writing to it. By waiting, the protocol ensure that there are no concurrent readers  at the instant that the writer success. How long should the writer wait, and how can he know? Temporal coherence achieves this by leveraging a global notion of time. It requires that each of the L1s and the L2 have access to a register that keeps track of global time. On an L1 miss, the reader predicts how long it expects to hold the block in the L1 and informs the L2. Every L1 cache block is tagged with a timestamp (TS) that holds the lease of that block. A read on an L1 block with a current time greater than its lease is treated as a miss
Each block in the L2 is tagged with a timestamp. When a reader consults the L2 on an L1 miss, it informs the L2 of its desired lease; the L2 update the TS for the block.
Every write is written through the L2; the write request accesses the block’s TS held in the L2 and if the TS corresponds to a time in the future, the write stalls until this time. The stalling is what ensures that no shares of the block exist when the write performs in the L2 cache, thus ensuring SWMR.
Protocol Specifications
The L1 has two states

Invalid
Valid
The L1 communicates with the L2 using getV(t),write writeV(T) requests. The first asks for a block and accepts a TS as a param. The write request asks for the specified value to be written through to the L2 without bringing back the block to the L1. The write(T) request is used for writing to a block that is  already valid in L1 and cries a TS holding its current lease as a param.

The L2 has four states:

Invalid - the block is neither in the L2 nor the L1
Private - the block is present in exactly on L1
Shared - it may be present in one or more L1s
EXPired - the block is present in the L2 but not valid in any L1

There is a corner case however where a writeV(t) message from a private block is delayed such that the block is now held privately but in a different SM. To combat this, every writeV(t) message, carries a TS with the lease of for a block and a match with the TS held in the L2 indicates a more straightforward case A mismatch indicates the latter, in which case the writeV(t) request stalls until the block expires, at which time the L2 is update and an ack is sent back to the L1. A writeV(t) or a write request received in sate S, on the other hand, will have to always wait until the block’s lease sate at the L2 expires.
Finally, an L2 block is allowed to be evicted only in the EXP state, because writes must know long to stall in order to enfroe SWMR.
Consistency-Directed Temporal Coherence
Temporal consistency enforces SWMR but at a significant cost.  Every write to an unexpired shared block needs to stall at the L2 controller. Since the L2 is shared, stalling can indirectly affect all the threads, reducing throughput. The idea is, instead of having writes be synchronously seen to other threads, can we make it async without violating consistency? A relaxed model such as in Relaxed Memory Consistency XC mandates only the memory ordering indicated by the programmer via FENCE. Such a model for wrtes to propagate to other in async manner.
When a write request reaches the L2 and the block is shared, the L2 replies back to the thread initiating the write with a TS associated with the block. We refer to this as Global Write Completion TIME GWCT, as this indicates the time until which the thread must stall upon hitting a FENCE, to ensure the write has become globally visible.
For each thread mapped to an SM, the SM keeps track of the max of GWCTs returned for the writes in the per-thread stall-time register. Upon hitting a FENCE, stalling the thread until this time ensure that all of the write before the FENCE have become globally visible.
Protocol Specifications
This is similar to the consistency-agnostic variant. The main difference with the L1 controller is due to the fact that write-Acks from the L2 now carry GWCTs. Accordingly, upon receiving a Write-Ack, the L1 controller extends the stall-time if the incoming GWCTs is greater than the currently held one for that thread. The main different with the L2 controller is that Write, requests do not induce a stall; instead, the write is performed and a GWCT is returned along with the write-ACK.
Summary & Limitations
The benefit with the latter is that it eliminates expensive L2 stalling. Instead writes stall at the SM upon hitting the FENCE. More omptimisation are possible to reduce stalling, however there are some critical limitations with temporal coherence.

Supporting a non-inclusive L2 is cumbersome, because the temporal coherence requires that a block is valid in one or more L1s must have its lease time available to the L2.
It requires global TS. With modern GPUs being large, maintaining a global TS may become difficult. A recent proposal however has show how a variant of temporal coherence can be implemented without using global TS
Performance is sensitive to the lease period. One that is too shored increases the L1 miss rate, and one that is too long causes the writes to stall for longer
Temporal coherence cannot take advantage of scoped sync. Store involved in CTA-scoped syn need to be written to the L2, but here, every write is to the L2 due to the write-through
TC involves TS which is complex to implement and to verify its correctness.

Release Consistency-Directed Coherence
TC is good but on  the other hand is cumbersome. Here we discuss a different approach to GPGPU coherence called Releace-directed Coherence (RCC) that directly enforces release consistency which differs from XC by distinguishing acquires from releases, whereas XC treats all sync the same.
RCC compromises on flexibility in that it can only enforce variants of RC, but is simpler and can exploit scope information and can be made to work with non-inclusive L2 caches.
RC: Non-Scoped & Scoped Variants
RC has special atomic operations  in one directed ordering by a FENCE. RS has a release (Rel) store and an acquire (Acq) load that enforces the following order:

Acq load → laod/store
Load/store → Rel store
Rel store/Ac load → Rel store/Acq load

Considering the message passing example as seen below: St2 as a release ensures that St1→St2. The acquire (Ld1) reads the value written by the release st2. Doing so the release syncs with the acquire ensuring the St2→Ld1 in the global memory order. This ensures that r2 will never be zero .
T1:
St1: St data1 = NEW
St2: Rel St flag = SET

T2: 
Ld1: Acq Ld r1 = flag 
B1: if (R1 != SET) goto Ld1
Ld2: Ld r2 = data1

// assuming that all is inited as 0 can r2 == 0 

In this model, without scopes, a release syncs with an acquire as long as the acquire returns the value written by the release regardless of whether the threads belong to the same or different scope. Thus, Ld2 will see the new value regardless of the fact that T1 and T2 might not belong to the same CTA.
A Scoped RC Model
In this model, each atomic is associated with a scope. A release is said to sync with an acquire if:

The acquire load returns the value written by the release store
The scope of each atomic includes the thread executing the other op

For example: a release of CTA scope is said to sync with an acquire of CTA scope if two threads executing the acquire and release belong to the same CTA. On the other hand, a release of GPU scope syncs with an acquire of GPU scope irrespective whether the two threads are from the same CTA.
To formalize this more, we can use partial order. Not all conflicting operations are ordered, only releases and acquires that sync with each other are ordered. This is how NVIDIA approaches this in the PTX memory consistency model.
Release Consistency-Directed Coherence (RCC)
This protocol will directly enforces RC instead of SWMR. This protocol does not propagate writes to other threads. Instead, writes are written to the L2 upon a release and become visible to another thread when that thread self-invalidates the L1 on the acquire and pulls in the new values from the L2.
We assume write-back/write-allocate L1 caches. Also, for now, ignore and assume that sync is between two threads from different CTAs. Later we talk about intra-CTA sync. The main steps involved in RCC are as follows:

Load and stores that are not marked with acquire or release behave like normal loads and stores in a write-back/write-alloc L1 cache
A Load marked acquire reads a fresh copy of the block from the L2. Then all valid blocks in the L1, other than the one read by the acquire, self-invalidate, ensuring Acq load → load/store

Exploiting Scopes
If all atomic ops are of GPU scope, the protocol works as is, because the protocol already pushes all of the dirty data to the L2 on a release and pulls from the L2 upon an acquire. The RCC can take advantage of CTA scopes: a CTA-scoped release need no write-back dirty blocks to the L2; a CTA-scoped acquire need not self-invalidate any of the blocks in the L1.
Protocol Specifications
There are two stable states:

Invalid
Valid
The L1 communicates with the L2 using GetV and write-back requests. GetV asks for a specified block to be brought to the L1 in valid state. This GetV does not carry a TS param; a block brought by the L1 via GetV is self-invalidated upon the acquire. The Write-back request copies the specified block from the L1 to the L2 without evicting the block from the L1. If the release and acquire are of GPU scope, the protocol must write-back all dirty blocks on a release and self-invalidate all valid block on acquires. R/A of CTA scope behave like ordinary stores and loads in a write-back/write-alloc cache.

Note: that the protocol does not rely on cache inclusion. A valid L2 block can be silently evicted without informing the L1. Intuitively, this is because the L2 does not hold any critical metadata such as sharers or ownership information.
Exploiting Ownership: RCC-O
Releases (force all dirty lines to  be written to the L2) and acquires (causes all valid lines to be self-invalidated) are expensive in the simple protocol. One way to reduce this cost is to track ownership, so that owned blocks do not need to be self-invalidated nor, written-back on an acquire/release.
The idea is to add an Owned state - every store must obtain ownership of the L1 cache line before a subsequent release. For each block, the L2 maintains the owner which refers to the identity of the L1 that owns the block. Upon a request for ownership, the L2 first down-grades the previous owner, causing the owner to write-back the dirty data. After sending the current data to the new owner, the L2, updates the ownership. Because a block is in the O state, it implies the absence of remote writers, there is no need to self-invalidate an owned block on an acquire. Because the L2 tracks owners, there is no need to write-back an owned block upon a release.
Even in the absence of scope information, ownership tracking can help in reducing the cost of intra-CTA acquires.
Protocol Specification
The main difference is in the addition of the Owner state. Every store in V or I sate has to contact the L2 controller and request ownership. Having obtained ownership, any subsequent store to that line is potentially stale at the L2. For this reason, when the L2 receives a request for ownership of a line already in the O state, the L2 first requests the previous owner to write-back.
Upon a release (CTA-, GPU- or non-scoped) there is no need to write-back dirty data from the L1 to the L2. Instead, the protocol merely requires that all previous stores must have obtained ownership. Upon acquire (GPU- or non-scoped), only non-owned blocks must self-invalidate. If the acquire is of CTA scope or the acquire sis to a owned block, it implies that the sync is intra-CTA and there is no need to self-invalidate.
Because the protocol hinges on the L2, maintaining ownership information an L2 block in O state cannot be silently evicted; instead, it must first downgrade the current owner, requesting a write back to the block.
Lazy Release Consistency-Direct Coherence: LRCC
In the absence of scope information RCC treats acquires and releases conservatively. In the RCC-O and intra-CTA acquires can be detected efficiently and handled but releases are treated conservatively. LRCC enables efficient releases. In LRCC, ordinary stores do not obtain ownership, only release stores obtain ownership on behalf of the store. When a block is released is later acquired, the sate of the block at the time of the acquire determines the coherence actions.

if the block is owned by the L1 acquiring thread, it implies that the sync is intra-CTA (no need to self-invalidate).
if the block is owned by a remote L1 it implies inter-CTA sync.

In the latter, dirty cache blocks in that remote L1 are first written back and the valid blocks in the acquiring L1 are self-invalidated. Thus, by delaying coherency actions until an acquire LRCC is able to handle intra-CTA sync very efficiently.
Protocol Specification

lit-notes/memory/Relaxed-Memory-Consiste.title: Relaxed Memory Consistency
lit-notes/memory/Relaxed-Memory-Consiste.content:
memory-model CPU
primer2020_2nd_edition
A relaxed memory consistency model is one where we allow the CPU to modify the order of the store and load operations between and inside of threads. The benefit of this is that, it can be optimized and increase CPU throughput. The downside is that we need to formalize tools to use in order to enforce that some operations cannot happen before others (e.g memory fences).
Example Relaxed Consistency Model (XC)
We will refer to this model as XC from now on. XC assumes that a global memory order exists as is true for strong models of SC and TSO, as well as the largely defunt relaxed models for Alpha and SPARC relaxed memory order (RMO).
XC provides a FENCE instruction that programmers can indicate when order is needed, otherwise, load and stores are unordered. Other relaxed consistency models call a FENCE a barrier, a memory barrier or a sync. Let core C_{i} execute some loads/store and X_i then a FENCE and then some loads/stores by Y_i. The FENCE ensure thats all the loads/stores of C_i will happen before any Y_i operations.  A FENCE instruction does not specify an address and two FENCEs  by the same core stay ordered. Note that a FENCE does not affect the order of memory operations on the other cores.
XC’s memory is guaranteed to respect (preserve) program order for:

load → FENCE
store → FENCE
FENCE → FENCE
FENCE → load
FENCE → store
And also implements sequential ordering whens loading from the same address twice or loading and then saving or storing to the same address twice.

This allows us to enforce sequential instructions within a core when needed.

lit-notes/races/Eraser.title: Eraser
lit-notes/races/Eraser.content:
Introduction
This software is to create a tool that can dynamically check for race conditions. It is based on Lamport’s happens-before relation which checks that conflicting memory accesses from diff. threads are separated by a synchronisation event. Eraser checks that threads follow a consistent locking discipline. A discipline is a programming policy to ensure no races (the simplest one being a mutex).
data race - when two or more threads attempt to access shared memory where at least one of the threads tries to write to that object.
Related work
Another way to do this was to use monitors, which are a group of shared objects together with procedures that are allowed to access them all grouped in a single anonymous lock that is automatically locked and unlocked at the entrance and exit of scope (similar to C++ lock guards).
Monitors thus provide a static, compile time guarantee that access to the critical section is serialised \therefore free of any data races. The issue with monitors is that they cannot help with dynamically allocated shared variables.
The issue with Lamport’s lock is that it cannot detect if a variable has been modified outside of a lock unless another one comes, causing potential races

even though y is shared, the happens-before would not spot the fault in this case.
The Lockset Algorithm
At runtime, a shared variables v will have a corresponding set C(v) which contain all the locks. Eraser monitors each that v has been accessed and which locks were held, if a lock was not held while accessing v, it is removed from the set C(v). The more the program runs the more accurate this set becomes.
upon access:
C(v)= C(v)\cap Lwhere L is the set of all the locks that are currently held. if C(v) becomes empty, then no lock is consistently protecting v which may lead to a data race.
L = all locks
locks_held = [all the locks held by thread t]
for v in shared_variables:
	C[v] = l
	
# upon access of v by t
C[v] = C[v].intersect(locks_held)
if (C[v].isEmpty()):
	raise Unprotected_shared_variable 
Improving the Discipline
you can have a shared variable that is inited once and then only read, or have read-write locks that do not need a mutex but can have multiple reads. That is why we want to loosen the discipline to support such cases.

lit-notes/races/FastTrack.title: FastTrack
lit-notes/races/FastTrack.content:
data-race  CPU
Intro
Multi-threaded programs lead to race conditions. In general, dynamic race detectors fall into two categories, depending on whether they report false alarms. Precise race detectors never produce false alarms, instead they compute the Happens-Before Relation for the observed trace and sensation and report iff the observed relation is represented using vector clocks (which are very expensive). Thus if the program has bn threads, the CC needs O(n) storage space and each op requires O(n) time.
Motivated in part by performance limitations, imprecise race detectors have been developed which may provide better coverage but can report false positive. For example erasor’s Lockset algorithm enforces lock-based sync discipline & reports an  error if no lock is consistently held on each access to particular mem lock. It may report an error however, on programs with alternative sync.
A limitation of static race detectors & imprecise dynamic ones is the potential for a large number of false alarms. It becomes difficult and time consuming to figure out which alarms are not false.
FastTrack uses adaptive representation of the happens-before relation to provide constant-time fast paths for the common case, without loss of precision or correctness in the general case.
A VC alg would record the most recent write to each var x by each thread t. FastTrack on the other hand exploits the observation that all writes to x are totally ordered by the happens-before relation and so it records info only about the last write to x, specifically to the clock and thread identifier of the write. The pair of a clock and thread id will be called an epoch.

lit-notes/races/HiRace.title: HiRace
lit-notes/races/HiRace.content:
data-race GPU instrumentation state-machine
HiRace
Intro
Data-races are very important and likely in the GPU due to the memory hierarchy. Most of the data-race checkers such as iGuard and Compute Sanitizer are NVIDIA specific and, compute sanitizer for example, does not detect global memory races. iGuard and its evolution heavily depend on NVBit  and does not seem to be actively maintained nor function on on later NVIDIA architectures from 2024.
This paper presents HiRace, which aims to serve the needs of today’s HPC and ML practitioners. HiRace works at the source level by instrumenting code via Clang’s source rewrite API. Source level instrumentation allows us to avoid reliance on compiler contracts and optimizations.
Design Novelties
Single Access Record: the most significant one and it should be sufficient to encode all necessary info about all prior accesses to identify races.  This design ensures that memory overhead is constant and small. In contrast, other designs maintain multiple accessor records significantly more mem.
Explicit State-Machine: HiRace achieves a modest size (const mem space per location) access history through use of an explicit finite-state-machine that encodes access history compactly.
Correctness: Having a state-machine allows the development of a Murphi formal reference model
Methodology
The design is based around the built-in sync primitives in GPUs (e.g __syncthreads) as opposed to focusing on the full generality of CPU parallel programming patterns. The methods do not preclude the handling of fine-grained thread sync, but focus on optimizing the most common and impact forms of thread communication in GPUs.
All of the relating possible thread access histories to a single mem location. For example, if a thread reads the same mem location multiple times, we do not need to record each access separately. A single thread ID and a flag indicating a read by that ID is enough. Even more, in a program with only two threads, if both reads concurrently read the same me location, it suffices to only track the ID of either accessor along with the flag identifying the multiple threads have read it.
In the general case, this would require 2^{T} flags to track all possible thread relations between T accessing thread. However, due to the mem hierarchy and asymmetric nature of shared mem scopes, instead of tracking individual threads, only the hierarchical scope shared by accessing threads needs to be tracked.
HiRace is based on a Finite State machine (FSM) that encodes the happens before logic introduced before. Whereas FSM is tailored to the current CUDA Programming Model it can easily be extended to other models with deeper hierarchies. This FSM has 25 states and 1200 transitions. They are sufficient to describe interactions of all atomic and no-atomic reads and writes so a single mem loc as well as needed syn history from warp-scoped and block-scoped barrier primitives.
Rather than dealing with each state of the SM, this sections develops similar state machine for simple concurrency models and two scenarios to show the key idea to this approach:

How the FSM performs with atomics
How the source of instrumentation works and is expresses as FSM transitions.

__global__ void noSync(int *data) {
	int i = threadIdx.x + blockIdx.x * TPB;
	int val = data[0];
	data[0] = i + val; // race
}
Take this program with no atomics and a race as one thread can read data[0] as the other writes to it. Here is how it would be described as an FSM.

They claim that this FSM will a singleo prior accessor ID is enough to track all races. To monitor data we create a shadow[k] entry for each array element. Each shadow entry maintains the following info:

Block-scalar clock
Warp-scalar clock
ID of acting thread
Most recent access (TID)
State of the FSM


Look at the following example:
__global__ void racy(int *data, int n) {
	int i = threadIdx.x
	int val = data[0];
	__syncthreads();
	if (i > 0) {
		data[i-1] = i; // race 
	}
}

lit-notes/races/Super-Collider.title: Super Collider
lit-notes/races/Super-Collider.content:
data-race GPU instrumentation recompilation
super-collider

compilation process to use SuperCollider.
Introduction
GPUs are becoming more and more popular in everyday compute, however data-races are still a crux for programmers. A data-race occurs when two or more threads can concurrently access the same memory without synchronization tools and one of the threads must commit a write operation.
Cuda organizes kernels into a grid of blocks which are themselves groups of 32 threads called warps. Each kernel can execute concurrently with other kernels. The thread hierarchy is mirrored with multiple levels of memory hierarchy, starting from global → shared → local, which means that a data race can occur anywher:

Between threads within a warp
Within warps in the same block
Threads form different blocks
Threads in different kernels
Threads in different GPUs
Threads in GPUs and CPUs

SOTA dynamic GPU race detectors operate by tracking mem sync operation performed by every thread in the kernel. Tools such as iGuard, Compute Sanitizer do it. However track all of that state is a tricky proposition. Many cuda kernel launch tens of thousands of threads collectively accessing multiple gigabytes of data.
Without a shock, iGuard and HiRace required up to 17x and 19x memory to store all of the metadata in order to track the mem.
This paper introduces SuperCollider which takes a stateless and sync agnostic approach to detect races in cuda applications, inspired by DataCollider. DataCollider applies a transformation to all weak loads and store in a device-side cuda code. The core idea: a compile pass expands every weak memory operation in the program (excluding strong mem and atomics) with two accesses to the same address separated by a random delay followed by an equality check of the values fetch from mem. The idea is simple: if back-to-back loads separated by a random delay return different values, then we can say that there is a data race
Because weak mem loads are the majority of GPU operations, SuperCollider is very effective. SuperCollider also, as a result, allows for cross-kernel data-race detection, across OS, between CPU and GPU and across multiple GPUs.
Methodology
Because there are so many threads with so many data access points, you cannot do random sampling. Instead, they chose a redudant-read approach and extend it to hand lost updates, leveraging peculiarities of SIMT and async mem operations. SuperCollider checks every weak mem spot.
Read Instrumentation: Clobbered Read
// pre compile 
mul vr0 = vr1, 4
add vr2 = %adrr, vr0
read.global vr3 = [vr2] // weak load
mul vr4 = vr3, 3.0 

// instrumented code
mul vr0 = vr1, 4
add vr2 = %adrr, vr0
read.global vr3 = [vr2] // weak load
nanosleep.rand 
readl.global.sys.strong vr5 [vr2]
if vr3 != vr5 {
	notify clobbered read error 
}
mul vr4 = vr3, 3.0

As seen, for all weak operations to the global, shared, or generic me spaces, the instrumentation preserves the original operation and  introduces a strong, system-scoped duplicate load. This prevents the compiler from reordering the duplicate but also bypasses the cache hierarchy .
The instrumentation also inserts a random sleep between the weak and strong load. Intuitively, the longer the sleep window, the more likely the technique is to expose latent races.
The compiler uses generic addresses, when it cannot disambiguate the memory space to which a pointer maps. Therefore, reads with a generic addr cant target local, shared or global mem. Local mem cannot lead to data-races, but it is not harmless to check.
Write Instrumentation: Lost Updates
// universal lost update 
write.global [%addr] = vr0 // original store
nanosleep.rand // shuffle warps
read.global.sys.strong vr1 [%addr]
if vr0 != vr1 {
	notify lost update
}

This is what the compiler inserts for weak write operations to the global, shared or generic memory space. It  mirrors the instrumentation for reads, but the approach checks whether another thread overwrites this thread’s update.
One way to also check is to include an additional write of garbage data to cover the case where two threads do have overwrites but the value they write is the same. This is mentioned in the next case
Write Instrumentation: Intra-warp Lost Updates
// intra-warp lost update instrumentation 
match vro = %addr
popcount vr1 = vr0 
if vr1 > 1 {
	notify lost_update
}

write.global [%addr] = vr2

GPUs rely on SIMT execution to efficiently amortize the work of an instruction over a warp. The snippet shows how SuperCollider leverages it to ensure that multiple threads in a warp do not write to the same addr.
The check use the match warp-collective operation to compare addresses across active threads and records if more than one thread write to the same addr.
Handling Async Copies
Hopper introduced Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA), an async copy engine that allows for high-speed, bulk data movement between the GPU’s off-chip global mem and on-chip shared mem without using any registers.
This is exposed via memcpy_async and in PTX with cp.async & cp.async.bukm. Because these instructions are async w.r.t the issuing thread, the executing thread cannot access the shared me destination without intervening synchronization. Hence, unlike regular weak mem access that maintains per-thread sequential consistency, async copies can create intra-thread races in addition to inter-thread races. Also, because these instructions touch both global and shared me, races may exists at either the source or target and the instrumentation needs to insert redundant reads for both.
Their implementation only covers bulk copies from share to global
Rejigerring Thread Scheduling
SuperCollider is blind to syncing protocols. Unlike state-tracking race detectors, if a race condition does not physically manifest at runtime, SuperCollider will not catch it. Therefore, SuperCollider uses techniques to randomly perturb sub-warp, warp and block schedule to expose latent races at runtime.
Warp & Sub-Warp Shuffling
The nanosleep performes two tasks:

Putting the active threads to sleep for some random amount of time
Switching the GPU’s scheduler to another ready sub-warp or warp
The Volta architecture introduced the threads-are-threads programming model used by subsequent NVIDIA architectures.

In this model, when a convergent group of threads in a warp sleep, the scheduler considers scheduling other sets of “ready” threads, either from the same or another warp, which can create conflicting sub-warps or warps, potentially exposing a data-race.
Block Shuffling
Consider the following example with a race between the first and last elements.
__global__ void 
racy_add(const float *A, const float *B, float *C, int N) {
	int i = blockDim.x * blockIdx.x + threadIdx.x;
	int ix = i == (N-1) ? 0 : i;
	if (i < N)  {
		C[ix] = A[i] + B[i] + 0.0f;
	}
}
On one end, consider a GPU with a single SM that executes thread blocks serially. SuperCollider would never expose the race for sufficiently large N, because the race would happen between different blocks. Even though in practice we could predict it, according to NVIDIA, thread blocks are required to execute independently, in any order or series or in parallel (i.e a well formed cuda kernel should have the same result regardless of the block execution).
SuperCollider injects a kernel header that allows users to perturb block schedules which we call block shuffling. The approach pseudo-randomly alters the architecture’s thread block schedule by rewriting blockIdx.x
\text{blockIdx.x}_\text{new} = (a\cdot \text{blockIdx.x}+b) \text{ mod } N_{x} 
where N_x is the grid size in the x dimension, a and N_x are co-prime and all blocks aggree on a & b. Block shuffling is then performed as a compiler transformation and does not require source code modification. However, it requires all code referencing blockIdx.x to be recompiled for correctness.
Summary
SuperCollider is very scalable and in the absence of races is totally stateless apart from the short-lived thread-local variables. SuperCollider can seamlessly detect races within a thread, between threads and within a warp, within a block and within a kernel.
Implementation & Usage
To use it, you must use a custom runtime and the other uses CUDA-GDB. Both rely on a modified compiler and the code must be recompiled.
When compiling use the --sanitize=supercollider

lit-notes/races/iGuard.title: iGuard
lit-notes/races/iGuard.content:
data-race GPU instrumentation
SOSP21_iGUARD
Intro
Background
Current GPU vendors have made features such as independent thread scheduling to make GPUs faster but in some case they can also introduce synchronisation errors.
iGuard is meant to be a tool to detect these race conditions while trying to minimise the run-time overhead. For these reasons it is directly on the GPU.
Note: a GPU program is referred to as a kernel.
The most basic kernels would use bulk-synchronisation where the data would get evenly dispersed among a max of 1024 equal-sized threadblocks (the GPU itself has hundreds of thousands of threads). The data in each threadblock is shared among the threads and is usually synchornised using a threadblock barrier syncthreads in CUDA.
However this fails for more advanced GPU kernels and features (e.g Graph processing). A modern way to do this is to introduce a scope of the threadblock data such that only local threads can see it. This has major boost in performance but in a producer consumer case it leads to a race. GPUs schedule threads in a threadblock in groups of 32-64 threads called a warp. Usually the progress is lockstep (each unit advances) together , but threads can deadlock if they use independent locks.
However with the introduction of Independent Thread Scheduling, it allows now threads in a warp to make independent progress. This means that application that relied on lockstep synchronisation would now need to introduce warp-level barriers syncwrap
Limitations of Current Race Detectors
current ones can detect races in scratchpad memory but not in the GPU’s global memory. Other tools do not support advanced features (e.g Barracuda does not support atomic operations).
iGUARD uses thread-fences to create locks even though the GPU does not support it. It can infer if the threads are coarse grained (one lock per warp) or fine grained. It then uses the lockset algorithm to detect race conditions.
Background
Current GPUs have a hierarchy  to scale hundreds of thousands of concurrent threads. A Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) is a basic execution block. Modern GPUs have around 100 and this block is usually SIMD. The SIMD units of a SM block share an L1 cache and scratchpad. The hardware decides the cache but the software decides the scratchpad.
Note: All SM share an L2 cache.
The global memory is accessible to all threads and is usually HBM or GDDR memory.
Race Conditions
Race Conditions due to Scopes
For CPUs a race condition occurs if we have a concurrent read and write and we need sync. For GPUs, sync alone cannot prevent a race of insufficient scope. In modern GPUs both atomics and fence can be qualified with a scope. These two operations can be combine to create scoped lock/unlock.
Consider a graph coloring problem where each thread assigns a color, one vertex at a time. Usually the number of vertices far exceeds the threads among a thread blocks which then perform multiple iterations to color all vertices in their partitions. Because the coloring depends on the number of edges, each block may take a different time to complete.
__device__ int getWork(...) {
	if (tid != 0) return -1; // leader thread
	
	currHead[blockId] = 
		atomicAdd_block(&nextHead[blockId],NTHREADS);
	
	if (currHead[blockId] < partitionEnd(blockId)) 
		return currHead[blockId];
		
	int victimBlock = getPartitionToStealFrom();
	if (victimBlcok == -1) return -1; // no work left
	
	currHead[blockId] = 
		atomicAdd(&nextHead[victimBlock], NTHREADS);
		
	if (currHead[blockId] < partionEnd[victimBlock])
		return currHead[blockId];
		
	return -1; 
} 
the kernel getWork shows how the leader thread obtains the next set of vertices to be colored. One may think that the block-scope atomic is sufficient (which in the common case is, when no stealing occurs). However if a thread block tries to steal work form the victim Block’s partition when the leader of the victim block was also assigning itself the next vertex set, a subtle scoped race arises. The thread stealing work may not see the update as it falls outside the block scope of the victim block.
Barriers & Scoped Races
Note that thread block barriers include the effect of a block-sopped fence. A barrier additionally waits for all threads in a block to reach it and thus can be slower. However, a race preventable by a block-scope fence is also prevented by a barrier.
Races Due to ITS
Any program that relied on lockstep execution and does not use __syncwarp() would lead to a race condition on modern GPUs due to Independent Thread Scheduling.
Here is an example
__global__ void reductionKernel(...) {
	if (blockSize >= 4 and tid < 2)
		sdata[tid] = mySum = mySum + sdata[tid+2];
		
	// __syncwarp(); <- needed to avoid a race 
	
	if (blocklSize >= 2 && tid == 0)
		sdata[tid] = mySum = mySum + sdata[tid+1]; // race!
}
This is done because without the __syncwarp, the first thread may move on and already check and modify sdata for the second time.

Design Overview of iGuard\
In-GPU Race Detection
All of the iGuard happens on the GPU without needed any hardware modifications. IGUARD uses NVBit which is a dynamic tool that enables inspection and modification of cuda kernel assembly code (SASS) on the GPU without needing to recompile. iGUARD performs two primary tasks via instrumentation:

Collects and updates metadata for active syn operations and accesses to global mem locs. The metadata is then used for race detection. It instruments sync operations (fence and barriers) and keeps track of their issuing thread warp and scope qualifiers. All loads, stores and atomics are instrumented to update the metadata
It implements race detection using information of the current instruction & metadata of the address of the access. Race detection happens on: loads, stores, atomics.

An in GPU detector needs to consider thousands of threads and their interactions (i.e via vector clocks) which is infeasible. Thus the mem metadata tracks reads & writes accessors, alongside relevant sync information, including scopes, for each unit of glob mem (4 bytes by default). Similar to ScoRD, the Happens-Before Relation is used to check if there have been conflicting accesses which are not synced.
This is also unrealistic, instead the thread and warp ID of the last writer & last accesssor is kept. This may lead to a false negative if a writer correctly is synced with the last reader, but based on the experiments, this is unlikely in practice. iGUARD also tracks if threads accessing a location are within a thread-block or span across thread-blocks to determine inappropriate use of scope.
To catch ITS related races, iGUARD tracks thread IDs beside warpIDs in the metadata and tracks warp-level barriers. It will report conflicting mem access within the same warp if they are or not separated by a sync (__syncthread() or __syncwarp()).
Inferring Locking Protocols
While there are no explicit locks in cuda, guides suggest using atomics and mem fences to create them. iGUARD can infer these instructions without needing programmer annotations. However, there is a new challenge since it should support ITS. under ITS some kernels employ per-thread lock within a warp (e.g. matrix multiplication), while others take one lock per warp, where a leader performs the sync.
To satisfy the goal of not having to need dev interventions, iGUARD infers the protocols used by a kernel at runtime by assuming a warp-level lock by default. However, it monitors if two or more threads from the same warp attempt to acquire the lock concurrently, which would mean that it is per-thread locking instead. Instead of the happens before relation, iGUARD uses the lockset technique which can detect races that do not manifest during and execution. However this is limited to locks/unlocks, thus the sync metadata is augmented with lock tables to infer locks locking protocols. The mem metadata is also augmented with a summary of locks held while accessing a loc.
Metadata Management
iGUARD requires 16 bytes of metadata per 4 bytes (4x mem overhead) and a total of ~2 MB of sync metadata. If the entire metadata resides on the GPU, it will constrain the kernel. Thus UVM mem is used. With UVM, memory is pinned (reserved) on the GPU. It is moved between the host and device on demand by the driver. Since only a small fraction is update & used for the race detection at a given time, UVM keeps the appropriate amount of data in device mem.
Optimizing Metadata Accesses
The challenge for in GPU race detection is the serialization of metadata accesses. Thousands of GPU threads can concurrently access a shared var. Accesses to the corresponding metadata needs to be serialized for the detection correctness. However, serialization can hamstring GPU software, thus iGUARD opportunistically coalesces metadata access due to react detection to reduce serialization. It also employees dynamically adjusted exponential backoff. It adjust the backoff length based on the number of concurrent threads at runtime to limit metadata to limit metadata contention while avoid not needed waits.
Note: this is what keeps the performance overheads so minimal for kernels with frequent acc to shared vars.
Race Reporting
iGUARD reports identities of instruction the address of the data participating in a race, & the cause. iGUARD allocates a 1 MB buffer to accumulate information of races without stopping execution on detecting a race. This buffer is sent to the CPU when full or when the program ends. It may happen that a kernel live-locks due to a race
Implementation of iGUARD
Metadata Layout & Allocation
the MD is similar to ScoRD but is extended for ITS & better for race detection accuracy & performance
Sync the MD
The active sync status of threads and thread-blocks are maintained in the sync MD. iGUARD keeps counters for diff sync ops to identify the latest sync op performed by  individual threads, warps & blocks. Specifically a block barrier counter is kept in each block and is incremented upon countering __syncthreads(). As well a warp barrier counter is kept for each warp and is incremented the same way. iGUARD keeps two thread-fence counters

One for block-scope
One for device scope
for each thread.

The thread fences are per thread since cuda defines the semantics of thread-fences to be per thread. Under ITS each thread may have executed different thread-fences at a given point. Finally, a lock table is kept to infer locks and locking protocols. The syn MD takes ~2 MB.
Mem MD
iGUARD keeps MD for each unit of global me. It tracks the identity of the accessor and access type to a given loc and sync information. The sync info is copied from the sync MD of the acc at the time of access. Instead of keeping all identities of accs, iGUARD keeps the MD of the last writer and last acc.
Allocating MD
while the sync MD needs only 2 MB, the MD incurs 4x overhead. To combat this cudaMallocMannaged() is used in order to alloc the virtual address without allocating physical mem. When the detector access the MD, page faults are triggered,; the UVM driver then allocs the physical mem for the page containing the MD. The driver also migrates this page between the host and device mem based on access patterns.
A drawback of UVM is the overhead of page faults incurred on the first access of the MD and the cost of migrating pages. iGUARD ensures that the overhead caused by UVM are incurred only if unavoidable. It keeps track of free mem on the device by tracking the amount of mem reserved by the kernel.
MD Updates
iGUARD instruments sync ops using the NVBit  tool. Look at the following code snippet
__device__ void instr_barrier(uint8_t **syncMD) {
	if (threadId < WARP_SIZE) {
		unsigned mask = __activemask();
		unsigned chosen = ((mask-1) & mask) ^ mask; 
		
		if ((1<<threadId) & chosen) // leader
			++syncMD[blkBarID][blockId];
 	}
	__syncthread();
}
This is an instrumentation code for updating sync MD on encountering __syncthreads(). One of the active threads, increments the corresponding block barrier counter. All threads in the block are synced thereafter. On encountering the __syncwarp, the warp the warp counter is similarly incremented.
__device__ void instr_fence(
	scope_t scope,
	uint8_t **syncMD, 
	uint64_t *locks
) {
	switch (scope) {
		case DEV: ++syncMD[DevFenceId][threadId];break;
		case BLK: ++syncMD[blkFenceId][threadId];break
	}
	activateLocks(scope, locks);	
}
This code snippet shows code on encountering a mem fence operation. iGUARD increments the corresponding thread-block or device scope fence counter for the corresponding thread. This is also part of the lock/unlock procedure.
